# Breach Radar 0.3.1

Reserving a workspace speaks the outreach v2 contract
(`undercurrent-ai/site` → `docs/OUTREACH_ACQUISITION_API.md`).

- **One claim code per contact.** When a card has contacts, a new checkbox on
  the Workspace tab gives each of them their own code, with a role suggested
  from their title (CISO, Deputy CISO, Head of IR, IT Director → admin; others
  → member). The codes are shown once, with copy buttons, and are not stored on
  this Mac — Helm → Acquisition reveals them again when needed.
- **The server picks the subdomain.** Leave the field blank and the name is
  reduced to a short, distinctive slug ("Sutter Health Vallejo" →
  `sutter-vallejo`); type one to override it.
- **Never a second workspace for the same company.** Reserving a company that
  already has a workspace — the same card again, or the same company from a
  different feed — adds codes for new people only.
- **Provenance travels with it.** Name, industry, ICP score, incident kind,
  filing date and board column go up as workspace metadata, so "why does this
  company have one" is answerable from the console.

Unchanged: with the checkbox off, the workspace carries the single org-level
code the third-touch template reads, exactly as in 0.3.0. A v1 server still
accepts everything this version sends.

## The store moved

Breach Radar is on the house app-data standard now. Your board lives at
`~/.undercurrent/db/breachradar/` and the app no longer contains any database
code — it shells to `cli/breachradar`, which owns the store.

Nothing to do, and nothing to lose: the first launch imports your existing
board, and the old `~/.undercurrent/breachradar/breachradar.sqlite3` is left
exactly where it is and never written to again.

What you get for it: every launch, release and install is recorded, so
`ucdb ls` can tell you which build you are running and since when; every write
carries an audit entry; and a Claude session can now read and repair exactly
the board you are looking at, with the same code the app uses, instead of a
second reader that has to be kept in step.

One safety change worth knowing about. The page hands the whole board to the
store on every change, which means a caller holding a short board is implicitly
asking for everything missing from it to be deleted. The store now refuses a
save that would remove more than about a third of the board, and says so. It
caught a real bug during this migration — a load that ran a fraction of a second
too early returned an empty board, and the next save asked to remove 84 cards.
Deletions are tombstones regardless, so nothing was actually lost.
